hypothesis: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly being used to automate and enhance the prediction of drug-target interactions (DTIs) by leveraging their robust inference capabilities and ability to process complex data representations, such as those used in deep learning models for binding affinity prediction. Recent advancements in LLMs have demonstrated their potential to drive and suppress human language networks, indicating their versatility and robustness in various applications (centaur_42, centaur_43). Furthermore, LLMs have been shown to automate cognitive modeling and scientific discovery processes, which can be applied to the prediction of DTIs (centaur_49, centaur_51). The integration of LLMs with deep learning architectures, such as convolutional neural networks, has proven effective in predicting DT binding affinities, outperforming traditional methods (deepdta_0).
